title: Chapter XLV

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth and Mrs. Gardiner visit Pemberley. Caroline Bingley tries to provoke Elizabeth by mentioning the militia (Wickham), embarrassing Georgiana. Darcy defends Elizabeth, calling her one of the handsomest women he knows.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter XLV,” how does Austen show jealousy at Pemberley? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XLV, how does Austen develop the idea of jealousy at Pemberley? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLV develops the idea of jealousy at Pemberley. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XLV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of jealousy at Pemberley. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XLV suggests about jealousy at Pemberley. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XLV to complicate the reader's understanding of jealousy at Pemberley. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of jealousy at Pemberley responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XLV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of jealousy at Pemberley follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XLV and its treatment of jealousy at Pemberley. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XLV as evidence for a larger claim about jealousy at Pemberley in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of jealousy at Pemberley. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: silence and reserve

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the chapter for characterization, irony (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this chapter suggest about jealousy at Pemberley? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Chapter XLV develops the idea of jealousy at Pemberley. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Darcy's reply to Miss Bingley shows how completely he has revised his first impression of Elizabeth. When the text says “it is many months since I have considered her as one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance” (Chapter XLV, paragraph 18), it shows this directly. In Chapter III she was "tolerable"; now he says "it is many months since I have considered her as one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance," a direct reversal prompted by Miss Bingley's own spite.

followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Darcy's reply to Miss Bingley shows how completely he has revised his first impression of Elizabeth. Useful evidence: “it is many months since I have considered her as one of the handsomest women of my acquaintance” (Chapter XLV, paragraph 18): Darcy reverses his "tolerable" of Chapter III. Theme link: Darcy reveals how far his own first impression has changed. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

items.text: A critic might argue: “Caroline's spite backfires, revealing Darcy's devotion.” How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the chapter.
items.lookFor: A defended position with evidence and one counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Darcy's reply to Miss Bingley shows how completely he has revised his first impression of Elizabeth. Useful evidence: “Convinced as Elizabeth now was that Miss Bingley’s dislike of her had originated in jealousy” (Chapter XLV, paragraph 1): Elizabeth reads Miss Bingley correctly. Theme link: Darcy reveals how far his own first impression has changed. items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Darcy's reply to Miss Bingley shows how completely he has revised his first impression of Elizabeth. Useful evidence: “How very ill Eliza Bennet looks this morning, Mr. Darcy” (Chapter XLV, paragraph 13): Miss Bingley's attempt to lower Elizabeth in his eyes. On characterization: At Pemberley Miss Bingley tries to embarrass Elizabeth by mentioning the militia, hurting Georgiana instead; after the visit she criticizes Elizabeth's looks to Darcy and receives a crushing reply. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
